strengths: The variable-specific state formulation addresses a meaningful limitation of stationary and global-regime models. Under the assumption that outgoing interactions depend on the source variable’s state, conditional summary graphs compactly represent up to K^N joint configurations using K graphs. This is a useful conceptual extension of amortized causal discovery.

The state-conditioned graph VAE provides a coherent implementation with shared interaction functions and amortized inference across sequences. Synthetic results demonstrate substantial benefits in some settings: for binary hidden-state linear data, Table 2 reports 97.08% summary-graph accuracy and 98.08% conditional-summary-graph accuracy, versus 60.45% summary-graph accuracy for ACD.

The evaluation investigates several relevant dimensions, including variable and state counts, training-data size, fixed versus learned decoders, and transfer across system sizes and basketball teams. NBA forecasting improvements provide evidence of practical predictive value, while the appendices supply substantial architectural and simulation details.
weaknesses: The comparisons do not adequately establish the advantage over methods designed for discrete regime changes. Regime-PCMCI, identified as the closest related approach, is absent from the experiments. Several evaluated baselines are explicitly described as unsuitable for the simulated switching dynamics. Moreover, comparisons against methods fitted to individual sequences also incorporate SDCI’s access to 50,000 training sequences. Comparisons with switching models on feasible settings are needed to distinguish the proposed contribution from these advantages.

The principal quantitative hidden-state spring experiment evaluates the union summary graph, which discards the state dependence central to the paper’s objective. Union graphs can also be dense, making raw accuracy misleading without class proportions and trivial baselines. For example, two independently sampled 50%-dense state graphs yield a union on which predicting every edge achieves 75% expected accuracy. Conditional-graph or time-resolved edge metrics, precision/recall, and majority baselines are needed to establish reliable state-dependent recovery.

The identifiability theorem requires a more careful statement and proof. Theorem 1 does not explicitly include the nonconstant-parent-effect assumption used in Lemma 2. Appendix A.3 then infers dependence conditional on all other lagged variables from causal minimality, which establishes dependence conditional on the remaining parents; the stronger conclusion requires an additional argument and suitable support assumptions. Furthermore, identifiability of the ideal SCM does not establish recovery by the relaxed amortized VAE, a limitation acknowledged in Appendix A.3 but obscured by the abstract’s claim that the approach recovers dependencies 'provably.'

The advertised scope exceeds the demonstrated hidden-state capability. The introduction suggests coverage of scenario classes 1–3, but Appendix F.2 explicitly reports failure with hidden history-dependent states and instead supplies state information during training. The stated inference model q(s_i^t | x_i^t) also lacks the history needed for general scenario-class-3 inference. These claims should be narrowed or supported by an appropriate temporal state model and evaluation.

The NBA results establish predictive improvements but do not validate causal discovery or show that causal correctness explains those improvements. A capacity-matched, state-conditioned interaction model with fixed or fully connected graphs would help separate graph discovery from architectural benefits. The forecasting protocol also needs clarification about ball information available during the prediction horizon and how observed player states are obtained during rollout.

Several omissions limit reproducibility and confidence in the comparisons: the meaning of error bars and number of independent training runs are unspecified; state and edge-label permutation handling is unexplained; Appendix C.2 introduces an undefined lambda; and baseline thresholds and linear-data rejection criteria are not sufficiently specified. The latter also affect the graph distribution and state balance underlying the reported accuracies. Separately, Appendix D.1 incorrectly presents singular values below one as necessary for fixed-VAR stability; the relevant necessary-and-sufficient criterion is spectral radius below one.
